citation.title: How Costly are Mark-ups in Australia? The Effect of Declining Competition on Misallocation and Productivity
citation.publisher: Reserve Bank of Australia, Research Discussion Paper 2025-05
citation.locator: Table 4 'Productivity Cost of Mark-ups', harmonic sales-weighted, row 'Change – ppt', p. 11 (PDF p. 17); measures defined on p. 10

entries.quote: Harmonic sales-weighted mark-up … Change – ppt 0.53 2.52 1.16 … This latter measure is similar to the overall value-added measure, but is narrower and only includes the cost of misallocation across firms, whereas the main value-added measure also includes ‘input misallocation’.
entries.derivation: Low = the narrower value-added measure, misallocation across firms only (1.16 pp); high = the main value-added measure, which adds input misallocation (2.52 pp); value = their midpoint (1.84), following the RBM convention that a range's midpoint is the central value (A-07).
entries.notes: The range spans two measures, not a confidence interval. The text (p. 10) rounds the narrower figure to "around 1.12"; Table 4 gives 1.16, which the library uses. F-C6-01 interpolates linearly inside 1.18 to 1.25 and never extrapolates (A-P06). The model is Edmond, Midrigan and Xu's, calibrated to Australian firm data; firm-level mark-ups cannot be estimated from public data. An oligopoly version gives 2.52 and 1.18 (Table 10, p. 16).

entries.quote: Focusing on the cost-weighted mark-up we can see that the cost went up by 1.54 percentage points when focusing on the narrower value-added loss measure, and 3.67 percentage points for the broader measure (Table 4).
